body.head: Journal of the British Society for Phenomenology, Vol. 17, No. 1, January 1986
body.p: THE CENTRAL GESTURE IN JASPERS' PHILOSOPHY

It is, I think, a constant characteristic of any deep philosophical system that you can recognize, in any of the work of its author, the same scheme of thought, the same spiritual “gesture”, whatever the topic he is in the process of dealing with. The reader may often get an impression of monotony, as if it could not have been “written in any other way”, as if he could have guessed in advance what he has just read for the first time. Such an experience has much to do with the Platonic “reminiscence”. On the other hand less profound thinkers tend to be far more unpredictable and each time invent with much ingenuity new solutions to new problems they are dealing with.

Karl Jaspers belongs to the first category. You can open any of his books anywhere and you will recognize “the sound of his thought” at once, whatever the topic may be. At the end of this talk I shall try to explain why, in philosophy, depth and monotony belong together.

The first move of Jaspers’ thought is oriented towards reality as that which is given in front of him, in an attempt to catch Being as a totality and a unity. But he fails. Any search for serious knowledge begins with dissociating “the world” into a plurality of aspects, of perspectives, which it is impossible to sum up in a unity, and which are also discontinuous due to the specific mode of each one of them. The evidence of any specific knowledge on one level depends in each case on the specific viewpoint and on the methods adopted — so that every particular knowledge is always relative to the definition of this aspect, of this viewpoint, of this method — it is never an absolute knowledge of the world as such. The world as a unity and a whole remains out of reach.

The first move is, then, an attempt which fails, not because of a mistake, but because it must fail. This failure is a creative one; it has the effect of throwing the subject back on to himself, as he is the point of departure of the attempt and of its failure as well.

What am I, as a subject which is confronted with “the world”? Here again, the subject would like to grasp itself as the being it is, as a unity. But it must recognize in itself, as a subject in the world and towards the world, the plurality and discontinuity of its own viewpoints and intentions.

The subject is alive, and as such it has needs and wants, it is threatened by death, it has vital interests for which it must fight. As such, it is also concretely located in space and time, under certain circumstances
